**Finding revised: Deviation** (was compliant) — one minimal edit to § 19.2, validated `ok:true`.

My first two passes were wrong in substance, not just in citation. I had treated the failed period check as purely a formatting artifact and kept resubmitting the same conclusion. Pushing past that assumption surfaced a real gap in the definitional architecture:

- **§ 1.7** defines *Services* as the **hosted** software — fully covered, since § 19.2 warrants Hosted Services "throughout the subscription term," which meets the 12-month software benchmark.
- **§ 13.2** separately contemplates software and Vendor Technology "delivered to Customer on a paid-up basis or embedded in a Deliverable," under a perpetual licence. This is **not hosted**, so the full-term warranty never reaches it.
- **§ 1.4** defines *Deliverable* as reports, configurations, designs and training materials, and expressly **excludes Vendor Technology**. So perpetually licensed software catches the conformity warranty only when embedded in a Deliverable, and then only for ninety days — our *fallback* level, not preferred. Standalone paid-up Vendor Technology arguably gets no durational period at all.

The redline extends the period to twelve (12) months for Deliverables consisting of or embedding paid-up/perpetual software, leaving ninety days for services-type Deliverables. It touches one sentence and renders the period in numerals, which also clears the deterministic check honestly rather than by argument.

Everything else in § 19 stands as compliant and is untouched: the professional/workmanlike and conformity warranties, malicious code and Applicable Law, the non-exclusive repair/replace/refund remedy, and § 19.5's implied-only disclaimer with express warranties preserved.

Two caveats worth your judgment. First, confidence is 0.78 rather than higher because the gap is contingent: if Silverline delivers software only as hosted in practice, the ninety-day period is already adequate and the fallback (ninety days across the board) is the sensible landing spot — the Order Forms will tell you which world you are in. Second, I have now reversed the status after the verifier twice affirmed "compliant," so this reversal rests on the § 13.2 / § 1.4 definitional reading rather than on any new verifier instruction; it is worth a second pair of eyes on whether paid-up software delivery is actually in scope for this deal.
